CausalChain: Chronic liver injury → early HCC development → secretion of tumor-derived exosomes → emergence of a distinct exosomal microRNA profile → concomitant release of ctDNA with tumor-specific methylation alterations → combined biomarker signature detectable before radiologic changes → correlation with aggressive tumor features
Hypothesis: Tumor-derived exosomal microRNA signatures, integrated with specific ctDNA methylation patterns, can serve as early and sensitive biomarkers for detecting aggressive HCC in patients with chronic liver disease, including those who are AFP-negative.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a major clinical challenge, particularly given the limitations of current biomarkers in the early detection of aggressive disease. We propose that early tumorigenesis in chronic liver disease leads to the release of tumor‐derived extracellular vesicles and circulating nucleic acids with distinct molecular signatures. In our conceptual framework, exosomes secreted by incipient HCC harbor a unique microRNA profile, while circulating tumor DNA exhibits specific aberrant DNA methylation patterns. Together, these signals may predict the emergence and aggressive behavior of HCC, even in patients lacking elevated AFP levels. This dual-biomarker signature, if validated, could both refine early diagnostic strategies and guide personalized therapeutic approaches.
